author: Mark Manson
description:
Stealing a cop car in Vice City might be one of the healthiest ways to spend your evening.

In the 90s, video games got blamed for everything. The kids who played the most hardcore games were often young, angry and depressed, so parents and schools assumed the games made them that way. Schools banned them. Governments investigated game companies. Ratings systems showed up.

That got the causation backwards.

Almost 30 years of research later, the picture looks very different. In Japan, a lottery decided who got a gaming console, and the winners saw mental health benefits comparable to jogging once a week.

Researchers at East Carolina University found a 57% drop in depression symptoms within a month of regular play. And a review of 24 studies covering more than 15,000 players found that gaming communities mostly improved friendships, social skills and social connection.

title: Playing GTA 6 Is Good for Your Mental Health

author: Mark Manson
description:
For practical, science-based advice that might change your life, sign up for my newsletter here: http://bit.ly/3JRg3NX

Studies mentioned in this video can be referenced here: 
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QYDAQMu_vLudNaq8UGNNUqi5q6EIs0O4S3BNj2LAbSI/edit?usp=sharing

---

Video games aren’t rotting your brain. The research says they barely move your well-being at all, but that research gets thin for the people who play the most, which is exactly where the problems show up. So I played the first few hours of GTA 6 to find where the line is, and it comes down to one question: do you feel more capable after you play, or are you playing so you don’t have to feel incapable?

Written & Directed by Mark Manson

Director of Photography Jess Choi
title: Self-Help Expert Explains Why GTA 6 is Good for Your Brain
